newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Accord paves way for Brazil Banespa sale.
newsitem.headline: Accord paves way for Brazil Banespa sale.

text.p: Sao Paulo state's troubled bank Banespa is closer than ever to being privatized following the settlement of a complex deal to restructure the state's massive debts.

Analysts say last week's deal to refinance Sao Paulo state's 24 billion reais ($22.4 billion) in largely unserviced debt to Banespa improves the prospects of selling off the bank to private investors.
"The bank's biggest trouble was the state debt. Once it is solved, Banespa will become attractive," said Manoel Maceira, asset manager at private bank Banco Tendencia.
Analysts said Banespa's strong pluses for potential investors include a 2000-strong branch network servicing three million customers in Sao Paulo, Brazil's richest state.
Banespa was put under Central Bank special administration in December 1994 due to financial troubles mostly stemming from Sao Paulo's state debt to the bank.
At one point the bank was relying on nearly three billion reais a day in Central Bank financial assistance to run its operations.

Like most state banks, Banespa was seen to have suffered from mismanagement. The bank was widely reported to have been milked by several state governors to fund electoral campaigns as well as to finance many projects on political grounds rather than economically sound criteria.

Following the example of Rio de Janeiro state's Banerj, Banespa, now in federal government hands, will be managed by a private consultant which will prepare it for privatization. The federal government expects to sell the bank by November 1998.

Up to now, however, Brazilian states have not had much success in their bank privatization drive. After two failed attempts last year, Rio de Janeiro state government now hopes to privatize Banerj on June 20 after it lowered the bank's base price.

Minas Gerais state, which is due to privatize its Credireal bank, had first expected to auction off the institution in April. But the state was forced to reschedule its plans as it took a long time for the Senate to approve a key loan to finance the bank's capitalization.
Minas Gerais now expects to sell Credireal in the second half of the year.
Despite the difficulties faced by other state governments, analysts believe Sao Paulo will have better luck in its bid to sell off Banespa.

A well-located, extensive branch network and a large client base are Banespa's choicest assets which will probably draw investors, especially foreign banks eyeing the Brazilian retail sector, they said.
With over 2,000 branches, Banespa is the sixth largest Brazilian bank in terms of branch network. Most of its branches are located in Sao Paulo, the country's wealthiest state.

Banking analysts also said the bank's client portfolio is likely to lure investors. Despite its financial problems, the bank said it managed to hold on to three million clients, just about one million less than Banco Itau, Brazil's second top private bank.
But chances for a successful selloff are far from certain as additional adjustments are needed to put the bank's books in order.
For one thing, the bank has not published financial statements since 1994 due to a court order, making it difficult for future buyers to determine the bank's current financial health.

Another key issue is personnel, analysts said. Despite recent staff cuts, Banespa still has 23,000 workers earning above market salaries. They said new owners, or the government, would have to slash salaries or cut staff to make the bank competitive.
